data.title: Hradiská – Svedkovia dávnych čias, a new volume on hillforts
data.excerpt: Slavic hillforts are proof that more than 1,000 years ago our ancestors could build defences which the greatest armies of their day often failed to overcome. The civic association Hradiská has now brought out a volume of articles by renowned Slovak archaeologists that also carries previously unpublished insights into the hillforts of Slovakia.
data.metaTitle: Hradiská – Svedkovia dávnych čias: a volume on hillforts
data.metaDescription: A volume of articles by renowned Slovak archaeologists on hillforts and life on them, initiated by the civic association behind hradiska.sk.

mediaTexts.alt: The cover of the volume Hradiská – svedkovia dávnych čias with a drawing of a hillfort gateway

children.text: Slavic hillforts are a symbol of the great building skill of our ancestors and prove that more than 1,000 years ago they were able to build massive defences which the greatest armies of their day often failed to overcome. They are also the best proof of the independence, sophistication, pride, wealth and political power of our Slavic ancestors. And not of theirs alone. Even before the Slavs arrived, hillforts were built by older cultures which lived in the territory of present-day Slovakia so long ago that in most cases we do not even know what they called themselves in their heyday, and we refer to them only by modern names invented by archaeologists so that they can tell their material cultures apart. Hillforts were often the seat of the elite. They were home to magnates with their families, to the military retinue, but also to skilled craftsmen – smiths and jewellers, whose products we can admire even today thanks to archaeology – to merchants, the clergy and other important inhabitants. Besides the dwellings of ordinary people, we find on hillforts the representative residences of the nobility, the first Christian churches and pagan sanctuaries. But we also find places of refuge that were used only when our ancestors needed to defend themselves against an attack by enemies. Sometimes they managed it, at other times it ended in tragedy. Behind every hillfort lie countless human fates, stories, moments of joy and of sorrow. When you visit some of them, their atmosphere will quite literally take hold of you.

For these reasons hillforts have attracted me from time immemorial, and I have always tried to learn more about them. Even though hillforts are real witnesses of ancient times, still standing today, we still know very little about them. When in 2009 I was looking for more detailed information about one particular hillfort in the Lesser Carpathians, I realised that for us laymen the way to it is well and truly barred. It is not at all easy to get hold of articles that deal in any depth with particular prehistoric and medieval timber-and-earth defences in Slovakia. Not to mention that until recently such information was almost entirely absent from the web.

blocks.alt: The volume Hradiská - Svedkovia dávnych čias

children.text: The wish to share information obtained with such effort with others was (besides the enthusiasm and the joy of uncovering long-forgotten places, and besides respect for the ingenuity and the abilities of our ancestors) one of the reasons why I began to devote myself to the subject of hillforts on an unobtrusive blog, where articles on individual hillforts gradually accumulated; in writing them I always tried to draw above all on the specialist literature and always to give the sources of my information. This approach probably contributed to the fact that the blog, and later the website www.hradiska.sk, which was originally intended for laymen and had no ambition to address the professional public to any great extent, gradually came to the attention of archaeologists, and I established co-operation with many of them. This co-operation has undoubtedly contributed to raising the scholarly level of our website, and in time it brought us to the idea that our civic association Hradiská, which had grown up alongside the website, should initiate and support a project to publish a volume of specialist articles by archaeologists devoted primarily to hillforts and to life on them.
The volume HRADISKÁ – SVEDKOVIA DÁVNYCH ČIAS is just out

The volume presented here, Hradiská – svedkovia dávnych čias, is the result of putting this idea into practice and the culmination of several months of intensive effort on our part to give the volume the proper scholarly quality and at the same time to make it accessible and attractive to a wider public. It was a great pleasure for me to take part in the preparation and organisation of the project. I believe the articles will please our readers as much as they have pleased me and the other members of our association. 
 
 At this point I should like to thank all the archaeologists who joined our project and provided us with valuable articles that also bring new, as yet unpublished insights into the hillforts of Slovakia. Great thanks go to the co-editor PhDr. Víťazoslav Struhár for his invaluable scholarly help in preparing and compiling the project, to PhDr. Vladimír Turčan, PhD. and PhDr. Marta Mácelová for the scholarly reviews of the contributions, and not least to the team of our collaborators who took part in carrying the project out (doc. RNDr. Kveta Markušová, CSc., Ing. Miroslav Bros, Mgr. Eva Gáborová, Mgr. Ľubica Sutton and Haden Sutton). For the financial grant we thank the Ministry of Culture of the Slovak Republic.

Work on preparing our volume on hillforts is coming to an end. From the table of contents attached you can see that the contributions were provided by renowned Slovak archaeologists. And believe me, every one of them is worth it. We shall start sending it out to those interested during January (around the middle of the month).
